title: {{NAME}} and the Dream That Needed Three to Tell It
moral: The most powerful magic is made when different kinds of wisdom work together.

pages.content:
There was a dream that kept coming to the kingdom of Thornmere every night for a week, visiting the sleeping minds of every child and adult and animal, always the same: a deep forest, a locked gate, a light behind it that was trying very hard to get out. No one could open the gate. No one in the dream had hands that fit the lock. Everyone woke from it with a feeling they couldn't name, something between urgency and longing.

Princess Solene had catalogued every report with the precision of someone who had read every relevant text in the Royal Library and found none of them sufficient. She met {{NAME}} at the palace gates with a journal so full of notes that it strained its cover. Her approach to the mystery was methodical, thorough, and completely stuck.

At the edge of the Thornmere gardens, sitting in the morning dew on a large stone with the patient air of someone who has been waiting for the right people to arrive, was a fairy named Cassiel. He was the size of a sparrow, with wings the colour of autumn light through amber glass, and he had been dreaming the same dream, he said, every night, except in his version he could see the light clearly. It was not a trapped thing. It was a seed.

And further along the path, half-hidden by white blossom, stood Solace, a unicorn the colour of first snow, watching all of them with dark, knowing eyes.

pages.content:
Solace came forward and touched her pearlescent horn to Solene's journal. The pages, which were dense with careful analysis, rearranged themselves gently, Solace's magic working not against Solene's thinking but alongside it, pulling out the pattern that was buried in all the reports.

Every dreamer who had walked toward the gate had approached alone. The dream was not asking for a key. The dream was asking for three.

Cassiel had known this from the beginning, he admitted with the gentle transparency of someone who had been waiting for the others to arrive at the answer so they could all reach it together. In fairy dream-lore, a lock with no individual key always had three holders. One to understand it. One to feel it. One to remember it.

'Understanding: Solene,' said {{NAME}}, thinking it through aloud, because that was how thinking worked best. 'Feeling: Cassiel. Memory.' {{NAME}} paused. Solace dipped her horn in a single graceful nod. Of course. Unicorns were creatures of deep memory: everything that had ever been, preserved in the spiralling pattern of a single horn.

Solene closed her journal with the specific click of someone storing one approach and opening another. 'Then we go into the dream together,' she said, with the matter-of-fact bravery of someone who has considered all implications and decided to proceed. Cassiel rose from his stone and stretched his amber wings. Solace lowered her head and waited. {{NAME}} took a breath that tasted of morning and whatever came next.

pages.content:
They entered the dream through the oldest method available: lying in the garden's oldest bed of flowers at the exact moment the morning light turned from silver to gold, each of them close enough to touch, all four. The dream accepted them without ceremony.

The forest was exactly as described, vast and dark and extraordinarily beautiful in its darkness, the kind of darkness that has depth and texture rather than emptiness. The gate was iron, enormous, set between two trees whose roots were woven together at the base like old friends who've stopped noticing they've grown into each other.

Solene went to the lock first. She read its structure the way she read everything: completely, systematically, from every angle. 'It needs the three movements at once,' she announced, stepping back with the exact information but not the next step.

Cassiel pressed his small hand to the gate. His wings turned from amber to something deeper, and a sound rose from him, quiet and pure, a feeling rather than a note. The gate shivered.

Solace stepped forward last and pressed her horn to the keyhole. The memory in her horn, generations upon generations of everything that had ever been, found in that lock the pattern of a very old promise, made before any of them had lived, and completed it. The gate swung open as though it had always meant to. The light that came through was warm and green and smelled like the first day of spring and every first day of spring before it.

pages.content:
The light was a seed. Cassiel had been exactly right, and he received this confirmation with the gracious pleasure of someone who has good taste in being correct.

A seed the size of a walnut, floating in a column of warm green light, turning slowly, humming with the particular frequency of something ready to grow but not yet sure where it was going. It was the dream of Thornmere itself: not a nightmare, not a warning, but a wish. The kingdom had been dreaming its own future, sending the image every night to every sleeping person until someone came to collect it.

Solene held out both hands. The seed settled into her cupped palms like something arriving home. Its warmth rose through her fingers and she looked at it with an expression that no entry in her journal had prepared her for, the look of encountering something true for the first time.

The dream forest began to change. The darkness shifted to amber, then to the specific gold of an afternoon in late autumn when everything is thinking about resting. The trees loosened their roots from each other, not breaking the connection but easing it, like old friends who trust each other enough to breathe separately. The light spread outward in waves and {{NAME}} felt it in the chest, in the way that real things feel: specific, and particular, and not like anything else.

pages.content:
They woke in the garden as the morning birds were beginning their second round of conversations, the ones where they've covered the essential news and moved on to more interesting topics. The seed was in Solene's hands in the waking world too, which surprised her in a way that lit her whole face from inside.

Solace was already standing, her coat back to first-snow white and her horn dark and resting, but with a satisfaction in her posture that suggested someone who has completed something important. Cassiel had fallen asleep curled in the crown of a nearby flower, which seemed fair.

'Where does it go?' {{NAME}} asked, looking at the seed. Solene thought for a moment, then walked to the oldest tree in the garden, the one whose roots had held the garden together for two hundred years, and pressed the seed into the earth at its base. 'With it,' she said simply. 'Where everything that's meant to grow goes.'

{{NAME}} sat in the morning grass with the sleeves of the lilac dress damp from the dew and let the morning perform its ordinary miracle of becoming. Sleep now, dreaming one. Let the world hold the seed while you rest. And tonight, somewhere in Thornmere, every person will dream something different for the first time in a week, and each dream will be only theirs, and all of them will be green.
